title: Children in langar
hook: children serve water and roll rotis
tomorrow: a seven-year-old on tabla: noise, or the start of kirtan?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a wide robe, fallen petals and a grandfather's gentle words at bedtime: stories at night. Today Fateh gets a job of his own.
screen: `STORIES AT NIGHT.` → `NOW FATEH GETS A JOB.`

segments.voice: Maya has never eaten at a gurdwara. Simran's best friend has heard about langar for years and finally said yes. She ties a scarf over her hair, leaves her shoes at the door, and sits down in a row on the floor. And the first person to serve her is seven. Fateh, holding a steel pitcher with both hands, tongue out in concentration, pours water into her cup and only spills a little. Maya whispers: wait, the kids work here?
screen: `MAYA'S FIRST LANGAR.` → `A ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `"WAIT, THE KIDS WORK HERE?"`

segments.voice: Her question is the old one: why hand a child the pitcher when an adult would be faster? The Sikh answer is that the serving is the lesson. Langar is the gurdwara's free kitchen, and everyone eats sitting together in rows, whoever they are. A child who pours the water learns that early, with his own hands. The Granth itself names a woman who ran the Guru's langar. On ang 967, in paraphrase, the bards Balvand and Satta praise Mata Khivi, Guru Angad's wife: she's like a leafy tree giving cool shade, and she hands out the langar's rich rice pudding made with ghee. Now a neighbor. Muslims read in the Qur'an, in Pickthall's translation, of the righteous who "feed with food the needy wretch, the orphan and the prisoner, for love of Him." The next verse, in paraphrase, has them say: we feed you for God's sake alone, and want no reward or thanks from you. That's real shared ground: feeding people for God's sake, expecting nothing back. And one honest difference. The verse names who is fed: the needy, the orphan, the prisoner. Langar doesn't ask. Hungry or not, rich or poor, everyone sits in the same row and gets the same food. Maya, who isn't in need at all, gets her water from a seven-year-old like everyone else.
screen: `WHY HAND A CHILD THE PITCHER?` · `MATA KHIVI'S LANGAR, ANG 967.` · `THE QUR'AN: FOR LOVE OF HIM.` · `ONE DIFFERENCE: LANGAR DOESN'T ASK.` · then, large: `SMALL HANDS SERVE.`

segments.voice: Count, on your fingers, the people who have fed you: whoever cooked for you as a child, a friend who brought food when things were hard, a stranger who served you once. Give each one a moment before you move to the next finger.
Children in langar. Kids pouring water and rolling rotis in the free kitchen, learning by serving.
Your line: small hands serve. A spilled drop is part of the lesson. See you tomorrow.
